results.name: conservative income
results.verdict: conservative income refused 17% of proposals and cost its owner money: the trades it declined averaged +12.0bps and the ones it allowed averaged -8.9bps, a gain of -2.09bps per decision over taking everything. Refusing 788 of 4528 at random matches or beats that in p=0.996 of 20,000 draws

results.name: aggressive event trader
results.verdict: aggressive event trader refused nothing across 4528 proposal(s), so it cannot have helped or hurt: on this sample it is not a mandate, it is a pass-through

verdict: 2 shipped mandate(s) over 4,528 real instant(s); the mandates disagreed with each other on 100% of them. NO MANDATE IMPROVED ITS OWNER'S OUTCOME on this sample. Divergence is real and demonstrated; usefulness is not. A mandate that refuses trades no better or worse than the ones it allows is enforcing a preference, not adding value, and saying so is the honest reading of this result. Usefulness here means beating refusal at random at the mandate's own rate, not merely showing a gain above zero — an earlier run of this module reported +0.35bps off 72 refusals and called it earned, and that gain does not survive the test. Note that a mandate which narrows every position loses less than one which does not, and that is sizing rather than selection: the utility figure above isolates the refusals by measuring each mandate against taking everything *at its own permitted size*, so the two effects are not added together.
